summary: Point Abino Light Tower, on Lake Erie's Ontario shore: a concrete tower built in 1917-18 after a lightship was lost off the point; automated 1989, relit 2017.

lens.note: Historic lens still in the lantern; it no longer turns since the 2017 relighting (LighthouseFriends).

structures.note: Height as 72 ft in the Lake Carriers' Association 1917 notice (via LighthouseFriends). The 87 ft in that notice is the height of the light above the water. The Fort Erie Observer calls the tower 87 ft; the station record's 30 m is not traced.
Built beside the tower in a style meant to suit the summer houses; sold by the town, now private.

access.note: Inside the gated Point Abino enclave; the road in is private. Ticketed walk-in visits to the exterior only, 21 June to 6 September, parking at 1010 Point Abino Road South, about 1.5 km on foot each way; no vehicles or pets past the gate; out by 6 p.m. Tours on hold for the 2026 season (Town of Fort Erie).

visit.note: Exterior only, ticketed walk-in visits; the tower is not open to climb.

facts.agency: Town of Fort Erie (owner since April 2003)

events.note: Lightship 82 placed on station off Point Abino on 3 August 1912, per LighthouseFriends. The 1912 Bulletin (PDF p. 31) says about 13 miles southwest of Buffalo Harbor entrance and names no point.
Severe Great Lakes storm, 8 to 10 November 1913
Buffalo Light Vessel No. 82 lost with all six crew in the November 1913 storm; wreck located 9 May 1914 per the 1914 Bulletin (LighthouseFriends gives 13 May); raised 16 September 1915
Tenders advertised in the year to 31 March 1917; the Lake Carriers' Association says the building was completed about 1 October 1917

About 1 October 1917, per the Lake Carriers' Association 1917 notice as quoted by LighthouseFriends. The station record gives 1918; no source read gives 1918 for first light. The Department's report for the year to 31 March 1918 still lists the erection.
Automated; Lewis W. Anderson stayed on as caretaker (LighthouseFriends)
Discontinued in 1995; dark until the 2017 relighting
Declared a National Historic Site of Canada; classified as a heritage building
Acquired by the Town of Fort Erie from Public Works Canada in April 2003
Restoration from May to October 2011 by Phoenix Restoration Services
Relit 1 May 2017 for the centenary, with an isophase switch giving two seconds of light and two seconds of darkness

corrections.why: The Lake Carriers' Association's 1917 notice, as quoted by LighthouseFriends, says the light went into operation about 1 October 1917. The Department's report for the year to 31 March 1918 still lists the erection, so the works ran into 1917-18. The Canadian register dates construction to 1917-18. A human should check against a light list or the Canadian Coast Guard List of Lights before changing the record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1918. LighthouseFriends, quoting the 1917 Lake Carriers' Association notice, gives operation about 1 October 1917; the Department's report for the year to 31 March 1918 still lists the erection work. The story attributes the October 1917 date to the Association and does not settle the record's 1918.
The 1917 notice gives a 72-foot tower with the light 87 feet above the water; the Observer calls the tower 87 feet; the record's 30 m is not traced. The story states the disagreement.
The 1914 Bulletin gives 9 May 1914 and 1.75 miles from the Buffalo light-vessel station; LighthouseFriends gives 13 May and nearly two miles off station. The story says May 1914 and gives both dates.

LighthouseFriends places Lightship 82 off Point Abino from 3 August 1912. The 1912 Bulletin says she was placed about 13 miles southwest of Buffalo Harbor entrance and names no point; later Bulletins call her Buffalo Light Vessel No. 82. Not settled; the story attributes the Point Abino placement to LighthouseFriends.
LighthouseFriends dates automation to 1989. The station record gives 1988, from a source we could not trace; the story gives 1989 and does not repeat 1988.

notes_for_editor: Keepers: the roster is LighthouseFriends alone. No Canadian annual report text we matched names these keepers at this station; the Marine lists are OCR-split and were not used for the names. Anderson's end year is 1989 in LighthouseFriends; another account reports 1990, not cited. Height: the 1917 notice gives a 72-foot tower with the light 87 feet above water; the Observer calls the tower 87 feet; the record's 30 m is untraced. First light: the record's 1918 is not supported by a source read; the 1917 date rests on the Lake Carriers' statement that the light went into operation about 1 October 1917 (as LighthouseFriends quotes it). Range: the 1917 notice says 'visible 15 miles' (not stated as nautical), so range_nm was removed. Characteristic: the 1917 light showed three flashes in twelve seconds; since the 2017 relighting it shows isophase, two seconds on and two seconds off (LighthouseFriends), so the record's Fl(3) W 12s was removed from facts as not current. Automation 1988 (station record) vs 1989 (LF); not traced. The 1998 register sentence ('operated continuously since it was built') conflicts with the 1995 discontinuance (LF, Town, Observer). Wreck located: 9 May 1914 (Bulletin 1914 p. 21) vs 13 May (LF). Lightship 82 station: LF says off Point Abino; the 1912 Bulletin (p. 31) says about 13 miles southwest of the Buffalo Harbor entrance and names no point; the 1912-1917 index (p. 25) says 'placed on station off Buffalo Harbor' for No. 82 (page 45 of the bulletin). Not settled. Access: the record says closed; the Town page gives ticketed walk-in exterior visits, 21 June to 6 September, tours on hold for 2026; the Observer quotes that the Town's insurer deemed the stairs too dangerous to go up. OCR table matches, checked on the page images: the 1917 tenders line, scan p. 47 (printed p. 40), on the Point Abino row; the 1918 erection line and the 37,770.65 expenditure, scan p. 33 (printed p. 34), on the Point Abino row, with Davieaux Island and Port Burwell in neighbouring rows. Wikipedia was read for leads only and is not cited. No photos supplied.
